message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and to ensure they receive a safe, habitable living environment. Below is a concise overview of key tenant rights under Texas law (Texas Property Code, Chapter 24 and related statutes). This is not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult a qualified attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Landlord must return the deposit (or a written itemized statement of deductions) within **30 days** after the tenant vacates, unless the lease specifies a longer period. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs or cleaning.
• If you receive a deduction notice, you can dispute it in writing and, if necessary, file a claim in small‑claims court. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a **safe and sanitary condition**.
• Must repair or replace broken plumbing, heating, electrical, and structural elements.
• Must keep the premises free of pests and mold. | • Report problems in writing (email or certified mail).
• If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or, in extreme cases, terminate the lease. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlord may increase rent only at the end of a **fixed‑term lease** or by giving **30 days’ written notice** for month‑to‑month agreements.
• No “no‑increase” clause can be enforced if the lease is for a fixed term. | • Keep copies of all notices.
• If you receive a notice that violates the lease or the law, you can dispute it in writing. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies.
• “Reasonable” means a time that is convenient for the tenant. | • If the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry and document the incident. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas’ own anti‑discrimination laws, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • If you suspect discrimination, you can file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • Tenants may terminate a lease early if the landlord breaches the lease or fails to maintain habitability.
• Tenants may also terminate a lease if the landlord fails to provide a written notice of rent increase or fails to comply with the lease terms. | • Provide written notice of termination and keep copies. | | **Retaliation** | • Landlords cannot retaliate against tenants who exercise their rights (e.g., by filing a complaint or requesting repairs). | • Document any retaliatory actions (e.g., sudden rent hikes, eviction notices). | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a **30‑day notice** for non‑payment of rent or a **60‑day notice** for lease violations.
• After the notice period, the landlord must file an **unlawful detainer** action in court.
• Tenants have the right to contest the eviction in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Keep copies of all correspondence and court filings. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter the premises without notice or consent, except in emergencies. | • If the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry and document the incident. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, the tenant may repair it themselves and deduct the cost from rent, provided the tenant gives written notice and the cost is reasonable. | • Keep receipts and provide a written itemized statement to the landlord. | | **Security Deposit Disputes** | • Tenants can file a claim in **small‑claims court** (up to $20,000) to recover a security deposit or damages. | • Gather evidence (photos, receipts, correspondence). | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, receipts, emails, text messages, and photographs of any issues. 2. **Written Communication** – Whenever possible, communicate in writing (email or certified mail) so you have a record. 3. **Know the Timeline** – Understand the notice periods required for rent increases, entry, and termination. 4. **Seek Assistance** – If you’re unsure about your rights or how to proceed, contact: - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** (for discrimination complaints) - **Local tenant‑rights groups** (e.g., Texas Tenants’ Association) - **Legal Aid organizations** (for low‑cost or free legal help) 5. **File a Complaint** – If you believe your landlord is violating your rights, you can file a complaint with HUD or the Texas Commission on Human Rights, or file a claim in small‑claims court. --- #### Quick Reference: When to Call a Lawyer - You’re facing an eviction notice and want to contest it. - You’ve received a notice of rent increase that you believe is unlawful. - You’re dealing with a landlord who refuses to make necessary repairs. - You suspect discrimination or retaliation. If you’re in any of these situations, it may be worth consulting a lawyer who specializes in landlord‑tenant law. If you need help finding a lawyer, let me know and I can provide resources.
